title: Americans Say the Economy Is Bad and Keep Spending Anyway. Polls Are Not a Forecast
excerpt: Confidence is at its lowest since 2014 while card spending runs 6.2% above last year. A former pollster's warning — that what voters and shoppers say is not what they will do — frames the final run to the November 3 midterms.
body:
• Consumer confidence is at its lowest since 2014, yet US spending rose in August — retail sales climbed 1.2% on the month, and Bank of America card data show household spending up 6.2% year on year in September.
  • The economy is the top midterm issue: 84% of registered voters told Pew it is very important to their vote, and CNN's generic-ballot average puts Democrats ahead 52% to 42%. The midterms are on November 3.
  • The gloom is real at the kitchen table, though: 64% of Americans in the October SSRS tracker rate the economy bad or very bad, and 59% say they are sticking to a strict grocery budget.
  • For Indian-American shopkeepers, restaurateurs and families, the practical read is to plan Diwali and holiday stock on card and sales data, not on sentiment headlines — demand has not followed the mood down.

Ask Americans how the economy is doing and the answer is bleak. Watch what they do at the checkout and the answer changes. That gap — between what people say in polls and what they actually do — is the central economic fact of the final stretch before the November 3 midterm elections, and it is the argument of a widely shared Fortune essay by Kari Butcher, Burson's chair for intelligence and insights in the Americas.

Butcher, a former pollster, calls it a category error. Polls measure what people say at a particular moment. They cannot, on their own, forecast purchases, loyalty or votes. A retailer who cuts inventory because confidence has fallen, she argues, may be pulling back while demand remains strong.

The Numbers Behind the Split

Consumer confidence is at its lowest level since 2014, yet spending rose in August. The hard data since then have kept the same shape. The University of Michigan's preliminary October sentiment index fell to 46.3 from 48.1 in September — close to the record low of 44.8 set in May — with survey director Joanne Hsu citing mounting frustration over the cost of living. The final October reading came in at 48.0, still down 10.4% on a year earlier, with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.7%.

https://x.com/arnaudmercier/status/2114454067980161449

Spending, meanwhile, has not cracked. Census figures showed retail and food-service sales up 1.2% in August, and Bank of America's aggregated card data put spending per household 6.2% higher in September than a year before, led by services. The National Retail Federation expects holiday sales to rise 4.2% this year to an estimated $1.013 trillion.

"Spending remained strong in August, but income growth is not keeping up. Many people are dipping into savings or using credit to continue spending, and that's not sustainable."

— Heather Long, chief economist, Navy Federal Credit Union

Why the Gloom Is Not Fake

The pessimism has receipts. The October wave of the SSRS Economic Attitudes Tracker found 64% of Americans rating the economy "bad" or "very bad" — up seven points since June and eleven points on a year ago — with one in four calling it very bad. Four in five are at least moderately worried about rising costs. Households are adapting in concrete ways: 64% have cut heating or cooling use, 59% are holding to a grocery budget, 58% are spending less on entertainment, and 46% are driving less. The New York Fed's consumer survey found inflation expectations rising and more households reporting they are worse off than a year ago, with gasoline up more than 27% year on year and AAA's national average at $4.37 a gallon. Spending is being defended, in part, with savings and credit — which is why economists warn the split between mood and money may close from the spending side if prices keep climbing.

The Midterm Trap

Politically, the economy dominates: 84% of registered voters told Pew the economy is very important to their vote, including 88% of Democratic supporters and 82% of Republican supporters. CNN's average of generic-ballot polls has Democrats leading 52% to 42%. Butcher's warning applies to campaigns and businesses alike — a generic-ballot lead is a measure of preference today, not a prediction of behaviour on November 3, and a confidence index is not a sales forecast.

What It Means for Indian-American Households and Businesses

For the diaspora, the practical consequences sit on both sides of the counter. Indian-American families are making the same trade-offs the SSRS tracker records — grocery budgets, fewer trips, deferred big purchases — while remittance and festive spending compete for the same dollars. Indian-American retailers, grocers and restaurateurs, heading into the Diwali and holiday season, face the inventory version of Butcher's question. The behaviour data — card spending up 6.2%, retail sales growing, a $1 trillion holiday season forecast — argue against stocking for the mood. The sentiment data argue for watching the till weekly, because if this gap closes, it will close in spending first.
